paper_title: Rare, Relevant, and Still Wrong: How Memory Fails LLM Group Decisions

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: When an LLM group's discussion is compressed into a short memory for a final decision maker, what should the memory keep? Two natural heuristics keep the rarest claims or the claims relevant to the decision criteria. On hidden-profile tasks both look attractive, because how widely a fact is held is confounded with whether it helps. We introduce CrossProfile, a diagnostic benchmark of 60 templates with automatically verified answer keys, in which the ownership of supporting, decoy, and irrelevant facts is crossed while their text is held fixed (480 tasks). Across Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and two DeepSeek models, both heuristics fail in predictable places. Selecting by relevance readmits decoys, because decoys are on topic: even a perfect relevance filter loses 23 to 31 points to rarest-first selection in the classic hidden-profile configuration. Rarest-first selection is no better than random selection on average and wins only where the rare facts happen to be the useful ones. In both cases accuracy follows the balance of evidence the memory keeps, not the policy that kept it. The decision model adds a third failure, a form of social proof: it gives extra weight to facts attributed to many agents. Removing the attribution tags, or reassigning them at random with line order fixed, raises accuracy in the classic configuration by 13 to 24 points. In natural discussions the evidence is lost before any memory acts: the complete transcript yields lower accuracy than no notes at all.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: An agent team may hold all the evidence needed for decision and still leave its final reader with the wrong information. Some evidence is never stated. Other evidence is stated and then lost when memory policy compresses the discussion. Even faithful memory can emphasize claims that the reader weighs poorly. An end-task accuracy gain alone cannot tell these failure points apart. Hidden-profile tasks make the distinction concrete: participants share some facts and individually hold other facts needed for collective decision (Stasser and Titus 1985; Gigone and Hastie 1993; Li, Naito, and Shirado 2026). natural response to repeated shared information is to preserve what few participants said. We study this response through rarest-first selection (R1), which ranks claims by the number of agents who stated them. The rule assumes that rare evidence is worth keeping. Faithfulness alone does not settle which evidence to keep. In one procurement template, supplier has passed every electrical safety inspection but took nine days to answer urgent repair callouts. Both statements concern the decision criteria. Keeping the favorable fact and dropping the unfavorable one can change the decision without introducing any false claim. What matters is the balance of the retained evidence, not only whether summary is accurate. Figure 1: Rarity and decision usefulness. Fact text stays fixed while the ownership of support and decoy facts changes; here irrelevant facts stay private. Filled dots mark the agents holding each fact, and the boxes on the right show what rarestfirst selection prioritizes. (c) The three ownership factors are crossed. Decoys are true, criterion-relevant facts that favor competing option. Role labels are never shown to the models. Figure 1 shows why the rarity assumption needs testing. In classic hidden profile, private evidence supports the correct answer and shared evidence favors decoy. Prioritizing rare facts can then help by keeping support, by excluding decoys, or both. If private facts instead favor the decoy, the same rule can damage the decision. On HiddenBench the two explanations cannot be separated: memory holding only the private facts reaches 91% accuracy on Qwen, whereas one holding only the shared facts reaches 6%, well below an empty memory. large gain for rarest-first selection there therefore says little about rarity itself. The obvious alternative, keeping the facts relevant to the decision criteria, faces the opposite problem, because decoy is relevant by construction. Testing either rule requires design in which fact prevalence and decision usefulness vary independently. We construct CrossProfile, crossed benchmark in which support, decoy, and irrelevant facts are each either shared or private. Within template, the fact sentences and their decision roles are fixed across all eight ownership variants, and the answer key follows from the fact roles and is verified automatically. Scripted discussions state every assigned fact, so memory selection can be studied against known inventory. CrossProfile is diagnostic benchmark: it isolates what memory policy and decision model do with known set of evidence. Changing ownership also changes when fact first appears, the holder tags attached to it, and its token cost, and we add control for each of these. Both heuristics fail in cells that the design predicts, and aggregate accuracy hides both failures. Relevance-first selection helps on average but loses 20 to 32 points in the classic hidden-profile cell, and perfect relevance filter loses as much, because relevance does not distinguish support from decoys. Rarest-first selection is no better than random selection on average; its advantage over random selection changes by 28 to 41 points depending on who holds the decoys, on all four models. Across policies, accuracy rises steadily with the net evidence lead of the correct option among the kept facts, and once that lead is known the policy adds little. The decision model contributes separate failure, form of social proof: it gives extra weight to fact attributed to many agents, although in our tasks shared facts were assigned, not independently observed. Removing the attribution tags, or reassigning them at random while keeping line order, raises its all-facts accuracy in the classic cell by 13 to 24 points. In natural discussions no memory policy beats another and the full transcript is less useful than an empty memory, so the evidence is lost before any memory acts. Our contributions are (i) CrossProfile, diagnostic benchmark that varies the ownership of support, decoy, and irrelevant facts while holding their content fixed; (ii) evidence on two open and two hosted models, with random-reference, fixed-item-count, and oracle-relevance controls, that relevance and rarity both fail in predictable ownership cells because neither tracks the balance of evidence; (iii) evidence that the decision model follows social proof in the form of holder tags, isolated from line order; and (iv) naturaldiscussion evidence that the main bottleneck lies upstream of memory.

sections.title:
2 Related Work
Hidden-profile research documents shared-information bias
and the difficulty of pooling distributed evidence (Stasser and
Titus 1985; Gigone and Hastie 1993; Lu, Yuan, and McLeod
2012); in the common-knowledge effect, information held by
more members carries more weight in the group judgment
(Gigone and Hastie 1993), and our decision model shows
a similar weighting from holder tags alone. LLM agents in
opinion simulations can also violate basic probabilistic con-
sistency, assigning probabilities to a claim and to its negation
that do not add up to one (Imel and Qi 2026). HiddenBench
adapts this setting to LLM groups and examines forced dis-
closure, passive summarization, and structured communica-
tion (Li, Naito, and Shirado 2026). With human groups, an
LLM facilitator increases how much information members
share without improving the final decision (Alsobay et al.
2025), which parallels our finding that disclosure and use
of evidence are separate bottlenecks. Our intervention holds
fact content fixed while crossing the ownership of decision
roles, and studies what survives a memory constraint applied
after the discussion.
sections.content: Multi-agent debate and agent frameworks study reasoning through interaction (Du et al. 2024; Smit et al. 2024; Wu et al. 2024), and collective biases in LLM groups can change non-linearly with group size (Flint et al. 2026), which our fixed four-agent design does not vary. Consilience intervenes during hidden-profile communication with calibrated controller that tracks evidence and redundancy (Babu et al. 2026). Communication interventions change what the group discloses; memory selection, which we study, determines which disclosed claims reach the final reader. Memory architectures maintain information across interactions (Packer et al. 2023; Park et al. 2023), and prompt compression and selective context address limited capacity (Jiang et al. 2023; Li et al. 2023). Benchmarks of conversational memory test long-horizon recall (Maharana et al. 2024), and recent multi-party benchmarks show that memory pipelines lose speaker and group structure (Yang et al. 2026; Hu et al. 2026); CrossProfile instead asks which evidence compressed memory should keep for downstream decision. Interaction-aware selection argues that records can matter only in combination (Subrahmanyam and Choudhary 2026), which is consistent with our finding that decisions follow the balance of the kept evidence rather than the merit of individual facts. Position effects further separate available evidence from evidence the model uses (Liu et al. 2024); our tag controls hold line order fixed to separate attribution from position.

sections.title:
3.1 Discussion, Memory, and Decision
A task specifies a description, candidate answers, and facts
assigned to agents. A shared fact is held by every agent; a pri-
vate fact is held by one. After the discussion, a memory pol-
icy constructs a memory for a separate decision call, which
receives only the description, the options, and the memory.
The decision call uses the same model weights as the dis-
cussion and sees the full transcript only in the REF control.
sections.content: Figure 2: Pipeline. Facts from template M01  (Table 4)  are distributed among the agents; HiddenBench tasks have three or four agents and CrossProfile tasks have four. After the discussion, memory policy compresses it under token budget B, either by summarizing the transcript (B3) or by selecting whole claims from claim inventory (R1, R1-rel, B4, Random). separate call with the same model weights answers from the task and the memory alone. Answer keys and role labels are withheld from all generation and from every memory policy except the oracle-relevance control. In controlled HiddenBench discussions, each agent is scripted to state its assigned facts. Natural discussions consist of initial individual votes, two rounds of messages, and final votes; memories are built from the messages, not the votes. Copy policies select from known claim inventory in the controlled condition and from an extracted inventory in the natural condition. In extracted inventories, claims contributors are the agents who stated it, which need not coincide with the agents who originally held the underlying fact. The summary policy B3 reads the transcript directly. Figure 2 summarizes these paths.

sections.title:
3.2 The CrossProfile Benchmark
CrossProfile has 60 main templates, five in each of 12 deci-
sion domains. Each template has four agents, three options,
and 12 facts: five support, three decoy, and four irrelevant.
Support facts favor the correct option, including negative
evidence about the decoy option. Decoy facts favor the com-
peting option, including negative evidence about the correct
option. Both concern the stated decision criteria; decoys are
true statements whose partial implication is misleading. Ir-
relevant facts concern other attributes and may be positive
or negative in tone. Each role group is independently shared
or private, yielding 23 ownership variants and 480 derived
tasks. Ten pilot templates are excluded from all main esti-
mates.
sections.content: The answer key follows from the structured facts: each favorable fact adds one to its options score, each unfavorable fact subtracts one, and irrelevant facts contribute zero. An automatic verifier checks every template for unique best option over all facts, decoy win when only decoy facts are counted, correct-option win when only support facts are counted, and the absence of hint words; all 70 templates pass. With the fixed fact counts, the keyed option scores +2 over all facts and each competitor scores 0. The task description asks for the best overall record on equally weighted criteria, but the decision prompt does not state the scoring rule. Accuracy therefore measures agreement with this constructed key. The controlled transcript randomizes the speaking order and the order of each speakers facts. Every shared fact appears in the first speakers turn, although not necessarily before every private fact in that turn, so first-mention selection is sensitive to prevalence. Copied memory lines keep their contributor tags and follow the policys selection order. Ownership thus changes how evidence is presented as well as its selection priority.

sections.title:
3.3 Memory Policies and Budgets
R1 orders claims by increasing contributor count, breaking
ties by first appearance. B4 orders claims by first appearance
alone. Random orders the same inventory uniformly at ran-
dom. These copy policies add whole claims in this order until
the budget is reached, skipping any claim that would exceed
it.
sections.content: B3, the evidence-preserving summary, asks the model to keep each distinct piece of evidence with its conditions, uncertainty, and disagreements. It receives word limit derived from the budget, and longer outputs are truncated to the budget. R1-rel first asks the model which fact texts concern the stated criteria. This filter sees the description, options, and fact texts, but no holders, answers, or role labels. Claims predicted relevant form the first tier and the remaining claims the second, with R1 order inside each tier; second-tier claims remain eligible. Since decoys concern the criteria, they are relevant by this definition. 5.2 Rarity Is a Bet on Who Holds the Decoys
Averaged over all ownership variants of CrossProfile, R1 is
no better than Random: 64.0% against 64.5% on Qwen and
63.0% against 63.4% on Llama (Table 2). This average hides
a reversal across cells. When support is private and decoys are
shared, R1 reaches 90 to 97% while first-mention selection
(B4) falls to 11 to 31%; when support is shared and decoys

5.4 The Decision Model Follows Social Proof
The all-facts memory is not a neutral reference. It contains
every fact and gives the correct option a two-point lead in
every variant, so a reader that ignored ownership would be
equally accurate across cells. Instead, accuracy is 21.0 points
[16.5, 25.6] higher on Qwen and 13.8 [9.7, 17.9] higher on
Llama when support facts are shared rather than private. In
the classic cell the all-facts memory reaches only 54.4% and
55.6%, about 40 points below the R1 memory built from the
same facts under a 60% budget (Figure 5).

sections.title: Upstream
sections.content: In natural discussions no memory policy is detectably better than another; R1 minus B3 is 1.4 points [5.0, 2.4] on Qwen and 3.1 [9.2, 2.7] on Llama (Appendix Table 16). The reason is visible before any memory is built  (Table 3)  . The full transcript (REF) scores below an empty memory on all three models, and the groups own final vote is correct in only 24 to 32% of discussions, although the same models reach 62 to 90% when given every fact. In DeepSeek-V4.1Flash discussions, string-matching heuristic finds private facts stated in full in only 1.7% [0.6, 2.9] of cases. Facts that were never stated cannot be recovered by any memory policy. prompt change helps one model only. Asking agents to state their evidence before recommending raises Llamas REF accuracy by +30.8 points [21.5, 39.5], and by +25.1 [15.9, 34.4] in paired ablation with fresh seeds, with no detectable change for Qwen (Appendix A.4). When the discussion carries more evidence, the memory policy matters again: under the evidence-first prompt, Llamas R1 memory reaches 57.1% against 22.9% for B4 and 53.2% for B3, whereas in the original discussions the three were within three points of each other (29.2%, 29.4%, 32.3%; means over budgets, Appendix A.4).

sections.title:
6 Conclusion
Neither rarity nor relevance is a safe default for the mem-
ory of an LLM group. In CrossProfile, rarity helps only in
the ownership cells where rare facts support the answer, rele-
vance readmits on-topic decoys even with a perfect filter, and
the decision model follows social proof, giving extra weight
to facts that many agents are tagged as stating. What drives
the decision is the balance of evidence between options that
the memory leaves, and how the reader weighs its attribu-
tion. Memory designs for agent groups should therefore aim
at that balance rather than at prevalence or topic, and should
not present how many agents stated a fact as evidence for
it when the sources are not independent. Evaluations should
vary who holds which evidence, and should check whether
that evidence reached the discussion at all.

Appendix A: Supplementary Results This appendix gives benchmark and policy details and all prompts (A.1), the full CrossProfile results (A.2), attribution controls (A.3), natural-discussion diagnostics and prompt ablations (A.4), measurement and statistical details (A.5), the hosted-model runs (A.6), and implementation details (A.7). A.1 Tasks, Policies, and Prompts Benchmark Construction and Example HiddenBench contributes 65 tasks: 58 have four agents and seven have three; 59 have three options and six have four. Its 503 facts comprise 250 shared and 253 private facts. Sixty facts contain several sentences and are kept as one unit. Controlled discussions disclose every assigned fact; natural discussions follow the benchmarks two-round exchange with initial and final votes. CrossProfile has ten pilot and 60 main templates. The 60 main templates cover 12 decision domains with five templates each: hospital equipment purchase (M01M05), school lunch vendor (M06M10), city bus route (M11M15), warehouse location (M16M20), software hosting vendor (M21M25), community clinic site (M26M30), job candidate for lab (M31M35), conference venue (M36M40), bridge repair contractor (M41M45), farm irrigation system (M46M50), library renovation (M51M55), and emergency shelter site (M56M60). Each main template has four agents, three options, and 12 facts. The support group contains three facts in favor of the correct option and two against the decoy option; the decoy group contains two facts in favor of the decoy and one against the correct option. The four irrelevant facts have two positive and two negative tones. The role structure is specified before the sentences are written, and facts receive neutral IDs in random order. Relevance refers to the stated criteria, not to whether fact favors the answer. Template M01 asks hospital procurement panel to choose scanner supplier, weighting purchase price, electrical safety, and repair response equally. The options are Brightline Imaging, Hallum Diagnostics, and Ostrava Clinical. Table 4 lists its facts with their evaluator roles. The eight variants change the ownership of the role groups while keeping every sentence fixed. Hallum Diagnostics took nine days to answer urgent repair callouts last year. Ostrava Clinical passed every leakage test on its scanners during the last audit. Ostrava Clinical engineers reach any ward within four hours for repairs. decoy support support support irrelevant Hallum Diagnostics has run an apprenticeship scheme for local school leavers since 2015. irrelevant Ostrava Clinicals headquarters was flooded in burst pipe incident in 2019. decoy support irrelevant decoy support irrelevant Ostrava Clinicals logo was criticised by local design magazine last spring. Policy Details The claim inventory records each claims text, its set of contributors, and its first-appearance rank. Each memory line is written as [A1,A2] claim text, and the memory keeps the selection order. R1 sorts by contributor count and then by first appearance; B4 uses first appearance; Random uses random order. M1 cycles through speakers, taking each speakers earliest unselected claim that fits, and then fills the remaining budget in first-appearance order. B3 summarizes the transcript instead of copying claims. For R1-rel, the filter is queried once per template, seed, and model, and its prediction is shared by all eight ownership variants. Statements are presented in random order. If no valid list of statement numbers is obtained after one retry, all facts are treated as relevant, which reduces R1-rel to R1. The predicted-relevant and remaining tiers are each sorted in R1 order. Copy policies add whole claims and skip claims that would exceed the budget. CrossProfile budgets price every fact with all four holder tags in template order, while selected lines carry their true tags, so the budget is the same across variants but the number of items that fit is not. Summaries are asked for at most max(1, B/1.3) words, and longer outputs are truncated to the budget at sentence boundary. Prompts The prompts below are used verbatim. Text in {braces} is filled in for each call (task description, displayed options, transcript, memory, or numbered statements); no evaluator labels are ever inserted. Line breaks between filled-in components are shown schematically. Decision call (all memory policies) SYSTEM You are careful decision maker. Use only the information you are given. USER {task description} {options} Notes from the group discussion. tag such as [A1,A2] at the start of line lists the participants who stated it: {memory} Reply in exactly this format and nothing else: Reasoning: <at most five sentences that weigh the options against the information above> Decision: <one option copied exactly from the options above> RETRY AFTER AN UNPARSEABLE REPLY Your reply did not follow the format. Reply again with exactly two parts: 'Reasoning: ' followed by at most five sentences, then 'Decision: ' followed by one option copied exactly from the options list. reply is valid if exactly one listed option can be parsed from it. Invalid replies are scored as wrong. Evidence-preserving summary (B3) SYSTEM You write memories of group discussions. Use only the information in the transcript. USER {task description} {options} Below is the transcript of group discussion about this decision. Each message starts with the participant who wrote it, and messages are separated by blank line. {transcript} Write memory of this discussion in at most {W} words for someone who must make the decision later and cannot see the transcript. Keep every distinct piece of evidence that was mentioned, together with its conditions and qualifiers, any uncertainty, and any disagreement between participants. State each piece of evidence once. Do not add recommendation of your own. Write plain text without headings. Output only the memory. {W} is the word limit derived from the token budget. Criterion-relevance filter (R1-rel) SYSTEM You sort statements by topic. Use only the information you are given. USER {task description} {options} Below is numbered list of statements collected in group discussion about this decision. {numbered statements} The description above names the decision criteria. Go through the statements one by one. statement concerns criterion if it tells us how an option performs on one of the stated criteria; statement about anything else does not. Collect the numbers of the statements that concern stated criterion and reply with one flat JSON list of those numbers, for example [2, 5, 7]. It must be single list of integers, not an object and not grouped by criterion. Reply [] if there are none. Do not add any other text. RETRY AFTER AN INVALID REPLY Your reply was not one flat JSON list of statement numbers. Reply again with only single JSON list such as [1, 4, 6], using only numbers from the list above, not grouped by criterion. The filter receives no contributor tags, roles, or answer. Natural discussion (HiddenBench protocol) SYSTEM {description} You have received the following information. Notice that the order of these facts is randomly shuffled; the order does not indicate importance or relationship. Please reason carefully: {information} Keep your response concise, just one or two sentences. {extra} INITIAL VOTE Please decide and provide your rationale in the following JSON format: { "vote": <A string, {possible answers}>, "rationale": <A string, representing your rationale> } FIRST SPEAKER, FIRST ROUND You are the first to speak. OTHER TURNS Previous messages from other people: {messages} It is your turn to speak. {extra} FINAL VOTE Previous messages from other people: {group discussion} {the initial-vote request above, verbatim} {information} holds the agents assigned facts and {extra} is the benchmarks optional instruction field. After the initial votes, agents exchange two rounds of messages. In later rounds each agent sees the other agents latest replies, including replies already updated in the current round; the final vote follows the last round. Memories are built from the messages, not from the votes. The prompt-ablation suffixes are given in Appendix A.4. In natural discussions, the claim inventory is built from the messages in two steps: every message is split into factual statements, and candidate pairs of statements with high word overlap are merged when the model judges them to state the same fact. Claim extraction (natural inventories) SYSTEM You copy factual statements out of message. Output JSON only. USER This message was written in group discussion: <message> {message} </message> List every factual statement in the message. Rules: 1. Copy each statement exactly as written. Do not paraphrase or join text from different places. 2. statement is one fact together with its conditions and qualifiers. If sentence only adds detail to the sentence before it, keep both sentences together as one statement. Example: "The bakery opens at 7. It also sells coffee." is one statement. 3. Leave out opinions, votes, recommendations and questions. If sentence mixes fact with an opinion, copy only the part that states the fact, exactly as written. 4. Keep the order of the message. Output JSON array of strings and nothing else, for example: ["first statement", "second statement"] RETRY AFTER AN INVALID REPLY Your reply was not JSON array of strings copied from the message. Reply again with only the JSON array. Duplicate check (natural inventories) SYSTEM You compare two statements from group discussion. Answer with one word: yes or no. USER Statement 1: {first} Statement 2: {second} Do these two statements state the same fact, with the same conditions and qualifiers? If one adds, drops or changes detail, number, condition or negation, the answer is no. Answer yes or no. sections.title: Implementation Details
sections.content: A.7 Local models are served with vLLM on two NVIDIA T4 GPUs. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Pro are accessed through the DeepSeek API (model identifiers deepseek-flash and deepseek-v4-pro). The order in which options are displayed rotates across seeds. We will release the code, the templates, and all generated discussions, memories, and model outputs upon publication.
